impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations for suits against the government in the Court of Federal Claims (28 U.S.C. § 2501) is subject to American Pipe class action tolling.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that 28 U.S.C. § 2501 is not subject to American Pipe tolling, recognizing that its prior decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's decision in California Public Employees' Retirement System v. ANZ Securities, Inc. The court affirmed dismissal of claims by bank holding company entities arising from the 2008 financial crisis for untimeliness.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides clarity for the government as a defendant—claims against the United States in the Court of Federal Claims cannot be revived through American Pipe class action tolling, reducing litigation exposure.
impacts.negativeImplications: Businesses and investors who relied on class action tolling to preserve claims against the government in the Court of Federal Claims may find their claims time-barred, eliminating potential recovery for takings and breach of contract claims.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a trial court must defer to the terms of an existing license agreement to assess copyright infringement damages, and whether the court's use of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine and assessment of non-compensatory damages against the government were legally permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the trial court's use of a hypothetical negotiation to assess copyright infringement damages rather than deferring to existing license terms, but vacated in part because the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the 'book of wisdom' and assessed non-compensatory damages against the government. The case involved government overcopying of TETRA® healthcare data interoperability software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Confirms that copyright owners are not limited to existing license rates when seeking infringement damages—a hypothetical negotiation may yield higher compensation, benefiting software companies whose works are infringed.
impacts.negativeImplications: The ruling that non-compensatory damages cannot be assessed against the government, and limitations on the 'book of wisdom' doctrine, may reduce ultimate damage awards in government copyright infringement cases.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations had expired on Insulet's Defend Trade Secrets Act (DTSA) claim for trade secret misappropriation related to former employees sharing proprietary design files with a competitor.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict and damages judgment in favor of Insulet, holding that the DTSA's statute of limitations had expired before Insulet filed suit. The case involved former Insulet employees who shared CAD files and proprietary information about insulin patch pump designs with competitor EOFlow. The court determined Insulet was entitled to judgment as a matter of law on limitations grounds.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides important clarity on DTSA statute of limitations analysis, potentially protecting companies accused of trade secret misappropriation from stale claims brought after the limitations period has run.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners face heightened risk of losing claims if they delay filing suit; companies must act promptly upon discovering misappropriation or risk forfeiting their DTSA remedies entirely.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages models and in overturning a jury award for breach of contract damages in a case involving automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to consider two damages models it had previously rejected. The court also reversed the district court's post-trial reduction of the jury's breach of contract award, reinstating it. The case arose from Ford's development of its own manufacturing configuration software (PDO) while licensing Versata's software under an expiring agreement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Expands options for trade secret plaintiffs to present damages models at trial and reinforces the sanctity of jury awards on breach of contract claims, strengthening IP holders' ability to recover for misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop in-house alternatives to licensed software face increased damages exposure if trade secret misappropriation is proven, as courts may accept broader damages methodologies.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied inter partes review estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting invalidity grounds that were not included in a prior IPR petition.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against two invalidity grounds, finding insufficient evidence to support estoppel on one ground and that the court failed to adequately account for hindsight bias on the other. The case involved a video game controller patent with back-mounted controls.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides significant relief for accused infringers by narrowing the scope of IPR estoppel, ensuring that defendants are not unfairly barred from raising invalidity defenses that a reasonably diligent searcher would not have discovered prior to an initial IPR petition.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face a more difficult path in establishing IPR estoppel to preclude invalidity challenges in district court, potentially prolonging litigation and increasing defense costs for patent disputes.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' in a provisional application to 'C1-C12-alkyl' in the issued patent constituted a correction of an obvious typographical error entitling the patent to priority from the provisional, or whether it added new matter breaking the priority chain.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating Enanta's patent covering coronavirus protease inhibitors, holding that the change from C2 to C1 in the definition of 'substituted' was not an obvious typographical error. Because the patent could not claim priority from its provisional application, Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (used in Paxlovid®) anticipated the claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Protects companies like Pfizer from patent claims where the patent holder cannot establish priority to a date before the accused product was publicly disclosed, providing certainty for major pharmaceutical products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical companies must exercise extreme precision in provisional applications, as even apparent typographical errors may break priority chains and expose patents to anticipation by intervening prior art.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a verdict form that combined infringement questions for multiple patents into a single question was reversible error, and whether the district court erred in its § 101 analysis of patents directed to wireless building automation systems.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, finding that the single-question verdict form covering all asserted patents was improper because it prevented meaningful appellate review. The court also vacated the § 101 determination for one patent and affirmed eligibility for others relating to wireless building automation improvements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Reinforces that patent holders asserting multiple patents must obtain separate infringement findings per patent, which may benefit defendants by requiring plaintiffs to prove each patent's infringement independently.
impacts.negativeImplications: Creates procedural complexity for patent plaintiffs asserting multiple patents at trial; combined verdict forms risk vacatur even after favorable jury verdicts, increasing litigation costs and delays.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using relay devices on farming equipment are patent-ineligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in finding the case non-exceptional under § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's patents directed to automated farming data collection and sharing were patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101, but vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional for purposes of attorney fee awards under § 285. The court found the claims directed to the abstract idea of collecting, processing, and sharing farming data.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in agricultural technology may benefit from broader § 101 invalidation of data-collection patents, and the remand on exceptionality may deter assertion of weak patents in the agricultural technology space.
impacts.negativeImplications: Agricultural technology companies seeking patent protection for data-collection innovations face heightened § 101 eligibility challenges, limiting IP protection for precision agriculture platforms and farm data systems.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed claim terms in a pharmaceutical patent covering dextromethorphan/quinidine combinations and whether it permissibly waived the Rule 65(c) bond requirement for a preliminary injunction pending appeal.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction preventing Hetero from launching a generic competitor to Nuedexta, upholding the district court's claim construction of the weight-to-weight ratio limitation. However, the court vacated the district court's waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal, requiring Otsuka to post a bond.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmance of the preliminary injunction framework that can block generic market entry before patent expiration, preserving market exclusivity.
impacts.negativeImplications: The requirement to post a bond pending appeal increases costs for patent holders seeking preliminary injunctions, and generic manufacturers face continued market exclusion during the patent's remaining term.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that grants an exclusive license but retains the right to sue third parties for infringement retains sufficient exclusionary rights to establish Article III standing.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains the right to sue for infringement—a right not rendered illusory by the exclusive license—has sufficient constitutional standing to bring an infringement action. The case involved warm-mix asphalt paving patents licensed exclusively to a third party.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners who structure licensing agreements to retain litigation rights can maintain standing to enforce their patents independently, providing greater flexibility in IP monetization and enforcement strategies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face the prospect of suits from both licensors and licensees when patent owners retain independent litigation rights, potentially increasing defense burdens and duplicative litigation risk.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of eligibility for certain patent claims relating to non-uniform constellation designs used in digital broadcast systems while affirming eligibility for others, and affirmed denial of JMOL on infringement and damages. The court found that some claims required further analysis under the Alice framework.
impacts.positiveImplications: Affirms that patents incorporating specific technical improvements to communication systems (like non-uniform constellations) can survive § 101 challenges, and upholds significant damages awards for standard-essential technology patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Consumer electronics manufacturers implementing industry standards may face continuing patent infringement liability for standard-compliant products, with limited ability to challenge eligibility of certain claims.

impacts.caseName: KG Dongbu Steel Co., Ltd. v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Court of International Trade erred in sustaining Commerce's remand determination that debt-to-equity conversions conferred no countervailable benefit, and whether Commerce's original determinations should be reinstated.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade and instructed reinstatement of Commerce's original determinations that government-directed debt-to-equity conversions for a Korean steel company conferred countervailable benefits. The decision restores countervailing duties on imported steel products, reinforcing Commerce's authority to evaluate equityworthiness in subsidy determinations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic steel producers and manufacturers benefit from reinstatement of countervailing duties that level the competitive playing field against subsidized foreign imports.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign steel producers and U.S. importers face restored countervailing duties, increasing costs for imported steel products and potentially disrupting supply chains for companies relying on lower-cost foreign steel.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB erred in its obviousness determination regarding sensor-based logistics tracking patent claims, and whether a third party's IPR petition filed on the deadline of the party sued for infringement raises time-bar concerns under 35 U.S.C. § 315(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination invalidating FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent claims and remanded for further proceedings. The case raised significant questions about third-party IPR petitions filed at the deadline of the party actually sued for infringement, though the court declined to review the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from closer appellate scrutiny of PTAB obviousness determinations, and the case highlights potential limits on third-party IPR petitions that may serve as proxies for time-barred parties.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that rely on IPR proceedings to challenge competitors' patents face uncertainty about whether their petitions will survive scrutiny, particularly when coordinated with time-barred parties.

impacts.caseName: TrackTime, LLC v. Amazon.com Services LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claim limitations reciting 'executable program code configured to' functions should be treated as means-plus-function terms under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f), and whether the district court's indefiniteness ruling should be reconsidered under intervening precedent.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the indefiniteness ruling on the '978 patent and remanded for further analysis under the court's intervening Dyfan precedent regarding whether 'executable program code' limitations invoke means-plus-function treatment under § 112(f). The court affirmed invalidity of the '638 patent claim on anticipation grounds.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software patent holders benefit from the court's recognition that 'executable program code' may not automatically trigger means-plus-function treatment, potentially saving software patents from indefiniteness challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers of software patents face continued uncertainty about how 'executable program code' limitations will be construed, potentially expanding the scope of enforceable software patent claims.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly dismissed a patent infringement complaint on obviousness grounds at the pleading stage and whether the case qualified as exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285 for attorney fee shifting.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal of the patent infringement complaint for failure to state a claim, finding the surviving patent claims obvious on the same grounds the PTAB used to invalidate other claims. However, the court reversed the exceptional case finding and attorney fee award under § 285, as well as the § 1927 sanction against plaintiff's counsel, finding insufficient grounds to support either.
impacts.positiveImplications: Raises the bar for courts to declare patent cases 'exceptional' under § 285 and impose attorney sanctions under § 1927, providing some protection for patent holders and their counsel from fee-shifting in close cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Affirms that courts may dismiss patent infringement suits at the pleading stage on invalidity grounds when prior IPR proceedings have invalidated similar claims, potentially discouraging assertion of weakened patents.
